prompt: A teammate says the token was only ever in a private repository, so a commit that deletes the line closes the matter. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Private repositories are indexed by search engines once they hold a secret
choices.why: They are not indexed. The exposure is the people and machines that already hold a copy.

choices.text: Every copy made before the deletion keeps the commits that carry it
choices.why: Right. The deletion is a new snapshot; the old ones stay in every clone, fork and backup.

choices.text: The deletion only takes effect after the next release
choices.why: Releases have nothing to do with it: the history is copied whenever anybody clones or fetches.

choices.text: Git keeps deleted lines in a log of its own that commits never touch
choices.why: There is no such log. The deleted line is simply still in the earlier commits, as they were.

prompt: Before the fix, in how many commits of the project's history did `git grep` find the administration token?
Which of these is not a secret, in the sense this lesson uses the word?

choices.text: A webhook's signing secret
choices.why: It grants something by being known: whoever has it can sign messages the receiver will trust.

choices.text: A session cookie pasted into a bug report
choices.why: Whoever pastes it into their browser is that user until the session ends. It is a secret.

choices.text: The public half of a key pair
choices.why: Right. It is meant to be handed out; knowing it opens nothing.

choices.text: A database connection string with its password
choices.why: The password inside it opens the database to anybody who reads the string.

prompt: Match each command to what it reads.

pairs.right: the files as they are on disk now
the lines each commit added, from the first commit on
what is staged for the next commit
the full snapshot of every commit

right_distractors: the branches that exist only on the server

prompt: `git grep` found the token in five commits, and `gitleaks git` reported it once, in the first. Why the difference?

choices.text: gitleaks stops reading the history at its first finding
choices.why: It went on to scan all five commits, as its own last lines say.

choices.text: Identical findings across commits are merged by fingerprint
choices.why: The fingerprint includes the commit, so the same line in two commits would be two findings.

choices.text: Later commits are packed, and packed objects are not scanned
choices.why: Packing is storage. gitleaks reads through git, which unpacks whatever it asks for.

choices.text: It reads only the lines each commit added
choices.why: Right. Four of the five commits kept the line without touching it, so only the first added it.

prompt: Your service's tokens are `svc_` followed by 32 random characters, and the code keeps them in variables called `ADMIN` and `PEER`. What should you expect from gitleaks' default rules, and what fixes it?

choices.text: They are found by entropy alone, whatever the variable is called
choices.why: Entropy is the second half of the generic rule; the first half is a keyword in the name, and these names carry none.

choices.text: The generic rule misses them; a svc_ rule finds them
choices.why: Right. No keyword in the name, so the catch-all stays silent, and a prefix of your own makes a one-line rule.

choices.text: Provider rules catch them by their length
choices.why: Provider rules match a provider's own prefix and shape; nobody wrote one for svc_.

choices.text: Nothing automated can find them; only a person reading the code
choices.why: A scanner finds them as soon as somebody tells it the shape, which is the point of the prefix.

prompt: Each finding carries an identity, made of the commit, the file, the rule and the line, and `.gitleaksignore` lists one of these per line. The field is called the ___.
Put the response to a pushed secret in order.
items: revoke the value, so it opens nothing
give whatever needs access a new value, kept outside the repository
remove the value from the code
read the logs for use of the old value during the window
decide whether to rewrite the history
add the hook and the pipeline stage

prompt: For linkbox, revoking the token and taking it out of the code were one change. Why could they not be two?

choices.text: The pre-commit hook refuses a commit that keeps the token
choices.why: The hook looks at what is added, and it was installed later in the lesson anyway.

choices.text: Flask reads settings once, when the code changes
choices.why: Settings are read when the process imports them; a restart with a new environment is enough.

choices.text: The running service compares what it receives against the value in the code
choices.why: Right. While the value is in the code, the running service accepts it, so revoking it means moving it out.

choices.text: The CI server accepts one commit per security fix
choices.why: Nothing on the server counts commits; it runs the pipeline on whatever is pushed.

prompt: With the new token in its environment, the service answered 401 to the old one and 201 to the new one. What did the 401 establish?

choices.text: That the history had been cleaned
choices.why: The history was not touched; every commit still holds the old value.

choices.text: That nobody had used the old token while it was valid
choices.why: That question needs logs, which linkbox does not keep. The 401 is about now, not about the window.

choices.text: That gitleaks would stop reporting the finding
choices.why: It still reported it; the finding is silenced only by recording it in .gitleaksignore.

choices.text: That the value every copy holds opens nothing now
choices.why: Right. That is the moment the copies stopped mattering.

prompt: A cloud access key was pushed to a public repository twenty minutes ago. A colleague is already writing the commit that deletes it. What comes first?

choices.text: Revoking the key at the provider that issued it, before anything else
choices.why: Right. Nothing else stops it working, and on a public repository the window is already twenty minutes long.

choices.text: Rewriting the history with git filter-repo and a forced push
choices.why: That changes one copy and leaves every clone and fork, and the key still works the whole time.

choices.text: Making the repository private
choices.why: Whoever cloned it in those twenty minutes keeps the key, and it still works.

choices.text: Waiting for the platform's partner programme to report it
choices.why: The programme may act, but waiting leaves the key valid; the lesson does not count on it.

prompt: Which statements about the token in `tests/conftest.py` are true?

choices.text: It opens nothing outside a test's temporary database
choices.why: Right: what makes a value a secret is what it opens.

choices.text: setdefault leaves a token that is already in the environment alone
choices.why: Right. A token set in the shell wins over the test's.

choices.text: pytest reads it before the test modules import settings.py
choices.why: Right, which is why the token is in place when settings.py looks for it.

choices.text: gitleaks skips conftest files, so it is never reported
choices.why: gitleaks has no such exception; the value is not reported because it does not look like a key.

prompt: After `git filter-repo` replaced the token in a fresh clone, which of these was still true?

choices.text: The CI server's copy still held the token, untouched by the rewrite
choices.why: Right. The rewrite changed one clone, and the server is another.

choices.text: The other commits kept their hashes
choices.why: Every hash changed: each commit's hash covers its parent, so the change runs down the whole history.

choices.text: The other clones would pick up the rewrite at their next fetch
choices.why: A fetch brings new commits; it does not replace a clone's history, and the old commits stay.

choices.text: An ordinary git push would replace the server's history with it
choices.why: filter-repo removed the remote on purpose, and replacing history takes a forced push.

prompt: In which case is rewriting the history worth what it costs everybody who holds a clone?

choices.text: Whenever a scanner keeps reporting a token that was rotated
choices.why: Recording the dead finding in .gitleaksignore stops the reports at no cost to anybody's clone.

choices.text: A customer's personal data was committed, and nothing can revoke it
choices.why: Right. Nothing makes that data worthless, so limiting its copies, together with everybody who holds one, is worth the price.

choices.text: Right after any revocation, so nobody can read the old value
choices.why: After a revocation the old value opens nothing, so reading it costs nothing.

choices.text: When the repository is public
choices.why: Being public widens the window; what decides is whether the thing committed can be revoked.

prompt: Why does `.gitleaksignore` name one fingerprint instead of switching off the `generic-api-key` rule?

choices.text: gitleaks has no switch for one rule
choices.why: Rules can be configured; the point is what switching one off would hide.

choices.text: A new secret in the same file is still reported
choices.why: Right. The fingerprint names one finding in one commit, and anything new has another.

choices.text: The fingerprint makes the scan of the history faster
choices.why: The scan reads the same commits either way; the fingerprint only filters the report.

choices.text: A rule switched off would also hide the finding from git log
choices.why: git log is not affected by gitleaks at all.

prompt: Why is the pre-commit hook a convenience rather than a control?

choices.text: It is too slow to run on each commit
choices.why: It scans only what is staged, in a fraction of a second.

choices.text: It misses files that are staged
choices.why: Staged files are exactly what it reads.

choices.text: Clones lack it; --no-verify skips it
choices.why: Right. Whatever is skipped or left uninstalled has to be on the server as well.

choices.text: It needs --redact to refuse anything
choices.why: --redact only hides the value in the output; the refusal works either way.

prompt: According to GitHub's documentation, which of these pushes would its push protection let through, on a repository with no custom patterns configured?

choices.text: A commit adding linkbox's lbx_ token
choices.why: Right. It looks for known providers' formats, and nobody told it about lbx_.

choices.text: A commit adding a GitHub personal access token
choices.why: That is a format GitHub knows well, the clearest case push protection exists for.

choices.text: A cloud provider's access key
choices.why: Cloud access keys have documented formats and are among those it recognises.

choices.text: A commit made with --no-verify that adds a payment provider's key
choices.why: --no-verify skips local hooks; push protection runs on the server and is not affected.

prompt: Which reason for putting `secrets` first in `ci/stages` carries the most weight?

choices.text: It is the slowest stage, so it should start early
choices.why: It is the cheapest: its scan of the whole history took 275ms here.

choices.text: gitleaks needs the virtual environment before the tests make theirs
choices.why: gitleaks is a single binary and uses no virtual environment.

choices.text: The tests would fail on the token otherwise
choices.why: The tests bring a token of their own in conftest.py.

choices.text: Its answer does not depend on the later stages
choices.why: Right. Whatever the tests say, a pushed secret is revoked, so nothing is gained by waiting for them.

prompt: Why does `ci/secrets.sh` pass `--redact`?

choices.text: A CI log is read by everybody with access to the builds, and kept long
choices.why: Right. Printing the value there would publish it a second time.

choices.text: Without it, gitleaks exits 0 when it finds something
choices.why: The exit status is the same either way: 1 when there is a finding.

choices.text: It makes the scan skip findings already in .gitleaksignore
choices.why: The ignore file is read with or without --redact.

choices.text: It hides the file and the line, which somebody outside the team could use to find the value
choices.why: The file and line stay, and they are what a person needs to act.

prompt: The image started with no token stops on a `KeyError`. A colleague proposes `os.environ.get("LINKBOX_TOKEN", "changeme")`, so that it always starts. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Nothing, provided every deployment sets the variable
choices.why: The proposal exists for the deployment that does not, and that one would accept a token written in the code.

choices.text: os.environ.get is slower than os.environ[...]
choices.why: The difference is irrelevant; the problem is what the default does.

choices.text: A deployment that forgets the variable runs with a known token
choices.why: Right. The refusal to start is the protection; a default turns a missing setting into an open door.

choices.text: gitleaks would block the commit, since changeme counts as a secret to its generic rule
choices.why: changeme is too short and too plain for the generic rule; the danger is not the scan.

prompt: Match each situation to the right first move.

pairs.left: the history holds a token that was already rotated
pairs.right: record its fingerprint in .gitleaksignore, with the reason

pairs.left: the hook refused a commit with a key in it
pairs.right: take the key out of the staged file

pairs.left: a provider's key reached a pushed commit
a customer's file was committed and pushed
pairs.right: plan a rewrite with everybody who holds a copy

right_distractors: make the repository private and carry on
